topics.title: Chanakya and the goals of economic administration
notes: Chanakya (Kautilya) was chief advisor to Chandragupta Maurya, more than 2,300 years ago. He combined economics, ethics, administration and public welfare.
Core idea: the prosperity of the king/state depends on the prosperity of the people. This is stated more explicitly in the Arthashastra; Chanakya Niti carries the ethical foundation.
Objectives: stable revenue, fair taxation, regulated markets, consumer welfare, prevention of exploitation, efficient trade, national prosperity.
Economic administration was both an economic necessity and a moral responsibility.
Deck detail: Chanakya Niti describes governance as serving the public good. Slide quote: "The prosperity of the state lies in the prosperity of its people."

topics.title: Five pillars of economic administration
notes: Taxation, Customs Duties, Tolls, Anti-Hoarding, Price Controls.

Deck detail (pillar descriptions): Taxation should be fair, moderate and efficient. Customs duties regulated trade, prevented illegal commerce and strengthened the treasury, while foreign trade was encouraged and national interests safeguarded.

Deck detail: Tolls (fees from roads, ports, ferries and marketplaces) funded public infrastructure and ensured secure transportation. Anti-hoarding protected consumers and maintained market stability. Price controls: the state monitored prices of essential commodities through appointed market officials, preventing exploitation and inflation and ensuring equitable access to necessities.

topics.title: Taxation
notes: Bee-and-honey analogy: collect taxes without harming citizens (elaborated in the Arthashastra).
Chanakya never supported excessive taxation. Taxes should leave people producing wealth, businesses growing, agriculture profitable, trade expanding, and citizens paying willingly.
Good taxation is fair, predictable, moderate, transparent and used for public welfare.
Modern parallel, GST: single system, easier compliance, broader tax base, reduced evasion, economic efficiency.

Deck detail: Taxation formed the backbone of state administration. Chanakya Niti advises safeguarding wealth, preparing for adversity and using resources wisely. GST parallel: single taxation system, easier compliance, broader tax base, reduced tax evasion, economic efficiency.

topics.title: Customs duties
notes: Mauryan trade was supervised. Imports carried duties for revenue and to protect domestic industries.
Objectives: regulate foreign trade, maintain quality, prevent smuggling, ensure accurate valuation, generate revenue.
Officials should be competent and tested before being trusted.
Modern customs regulate imports, exports, anti-dumping duties, national security and trade policy.
Deck detail: Chanakya believed wealth enters the kingdom through productive commerce but should be regulated by capable administrators.

topics.title: Tolls and infrastructure financing
notes: Tolls on roads, bridges, ports, ferries and routes paid for road maintenance, public infrastructure, military movement, trade facilitation and administrative efficiency.
Tolls were seen as payment for public services, unlike arbitrary taxes.
Good infrastructure brings lower transport costs, faster trade, development and employment.
Modern examples: highway tolls, airport user charges, port fees. Principle: users pay to maintain infrastructure.
Deck detail: Roads, bridges, ports, ferries and trade routes required maintenance; travellers and merchants using these facilities paid tolls.

topics.title: Price regulation
notes: Officials monitored market prices, quality, weights, measures and supply conditions.
Objectives: protect consumers, prevent inflation, ensure fairness, discourage profiteering.
The ruler must intervene when market forces create injustice.
Deck detail: Markets cannot function efficiently if sellers manipulate prices, so Chanakya believed markets require supervision.

topics.title: Anti-hoarding
notes: Artificial scarcity: traders store goods, reduce supply, raise prices and earn abnormal profits.
Officials monitored inventories, and illegal stockpiling was punished.
Aim: stable prices, uninterrupted supply, food security, public confidence.
Modern emergency controls cover food grains, medicines, fertilizers, oxygen cylinders and fuel.
Deck detail: Chanakya considered hoarding harmful because it hurt ordinary citizens. Modern principle: markets should not exploit public suffering.

topics.title: Public welfare as the centre of policy
notes: Wealth is not an end in itself.
A prosperous state has educated citizens, secure trade, agricultural growth, efficient administration, honest officials and stable markets.
Public welfare includes law and order, employment, food security, fair justice, infrastructure and trade promotion.
Deck detail: Chanakya repeatedly advises prudent management of wealth, learning and resources and encourages preparation for future uncertainties. Economic prosperity and social welfare go together.

Deck detail (Chanakya's Vision): a strong economy is built on ethical governance, fair markets, disciplined trade and the welfare of every citizen. Modern relevance: GST, customs regulations, anti-hoarding laws, consumer protection legislation and government price stabilization policies.

topics.title: Ancient principle → modern equivalent
notes: Fair Taxation → GST
Customs Duties → Customs Act
Tolls → National Highway Authority
Price Regulation → Consumer Protection Act
Anti-Hoarding → Essential Commodities Act
Honest Officials → Civil Services & Vigilance
Market Inspection → Consumer Affairs Department
Trade Regulation → Competition Commission of India
Second table: preventing monopolies, hoarding and unfair practices → Competition Act 2002 & CCI. Protecting consumers through prices and quality → Consumer Protection Act 2019.

Deck detail (common objectives): fair and moderate taxation / GST - simplify taxation, improve compliance and ensure steady revenue without burdening businesses. Preventing monopolies, hoarding and unfair trade practices / Competition Act 2002 & CCI - promote healthy competition, prevent market abuse and protect economic efficiency. Protecting consumers through regulated prices and quality standards / Consumer Protection Act 2019 - safeguard consumer rights, ensure fair trade practices and provide grievance redressal.

topics.title: Case study: onion price crisis
notes: Rain damages crops. Wholesalers secretly store onions, and retail price rises from ₹25 to ₹120/kg.
Farmers don't gain because middlemen bought the crop earlier.
This will be used for scenario questions about artificial scarcity, hoarding and the state's role. Only slide-supported answers will be used.

modules.title: India's Position in the Ancient Global Trade Network

topics.title: Trade routes (concept)
notes: Trade routes are the pathways connecting settlements, territories and landscapes.
States sought to develop and control them.
The Silk Route (overland across Asia) and the Spice Route (Indian Ocean) were the earliest extensive networks linking Africa, Asia and Europe.

topics.title: Importance of India
notes: India held a strategic position between East and West.
Northwest passes: Karakoram, Burzil, Lanak La, Zoji La. Northeast passes: Thang La, Tulung La, Dom La, Andra La. These linked India to Central Asia, Tibet and China.
Uttarapatha ran from Tamralipti (Tamluk) to the Oxus. It linked Champa, Pataliputra, Kasi, Kausambi, Mathura, Sakala (Sialkot), Taxila, Purushapura (Peshawar), Kapisa (Begram) and Balkh.
A central-plateau route linked Kausambi and Mathura with Ujjayini and Bharukachha (Barygaza).
The Indian Ocean sits at the centre of maritime networks, encircled by Africa, Europe and Asia.
Coastline is given as 11,098.8 km in this deck (see FLAG 1).
Lagoons and sheltered waters favoured port development.
Harappans were the earliest mariners. Using monsoon winds, they sailed from Gujarat and the Makran coast to Oman, Bahrain and West Asia.

topics.title: Harappan trade routes
notes: Internal routes:
Sindh–South Baluchistan via the Kirthar mountains
Coastal Sindh–Upper Sindh–Central Indus plains
Punjab–East Punjab–Rajasthan via Cholistan
Sindh–Gujarat
Sindh–Baluchistan via Kachchh and Kathiawar
Coastal route: Gujarat (Lothal, Dholavira) to the Makran coast (Sutkagendor).
Materials: shell, copper, gold, lead, zinc, alabaster, limestone, steatite, carnelian, agate, jasper. These were processed at manufacturing centres.
External route: via Iran and Afghanistan into West and Central Asia.

topics.title: Maritime trade and maritime archaeology
notes: Anuradhapura excavation: Brahmi script was introduced to Sri Lanka by Indian traders, probably in the 5th–4th century BC.
Brahmi and Kharoshti inscriptions (1st–5th century AD) at Tamralipti and West Bengal show Bengal had contacts with northwest India.
Traders from Gandhara and the Oxus reached Mathura and the Gangetic valley overland, then sailed to Southeast Asia.
Kharoshti-Brahmi inscriptions in Bengal, Odisha, Thailand, Vietnam, Bali and Funan suggest script and language migrated with the horse trade.
Ceramic evidence (Rouletted ware) is found across the subcontinent, Southeast Asia and West Asia.
In the early centuries CE, mariners of India, Southeast Asia, the Red Sea, the Persian Gulf and the Mediterranean were interlinked.
Ban Don Ta Phet (Thailand) excavations date India–Southeast Asia contact to the 4th century BCE.
Imports:
High-bronze tin: yellow and gold-like, used for coinage, mainly sourced from Thailand.
Spices from the eastern Indonesian islands.
Chola naval expedition: exports were pearls, pepper and textiles; imports were camphor, copper and tin.

topics.title: Caravan trade
notes: Trading infrastructure developed with the rise of the 16 Mahajanapadas.
A caravan was a group of merchants travelling together for safety.
Pack animals: camels, horses, bullocks, donkeys.
Infrastructure: inns/serais, wells, fortified outposts.
The earliest Indian reference to a caravanserai is Ashoka's Delhi-Topra pillar edict No. 7 (3rd century BCE).
Mauryan routes reached Southeast Asia through the Malay Peninsula. The Khyber Pass was a key gateway.
Exports:
Silk and textiles (cotton, muslin, embroidered garments)
Spices (pepper, cinnamon, cardamom)
Exotic foods
Gems (diamonds, pearls, sapphires)
Ivory, timber, bamboo, dyes
Wootz steel and medicinal substances
Imports: lead, wine, horses, crude glass, asphalt, antimony.

topics.title: Inland routes
notes: Major trade centres: Barygaza, Ujjaini, Muziris, Soppara, Pataliputra, Kalyana, Poduca, Kaveripattinam, Tamralipti.
The two major routes were Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha.
"Uttarapatha" is mentioned mainly in Panini's Ashtadhyayi.
Uttarapatha was a land-river route from northwest India across the Indo-Gangetic plain to Tamralipti on the Bay of Bengal.
Northern path: Lahore, Jalandhar, Saharanpur, Bijnor, Gorakhpur, Bihar, Bengal.
Southern path: Lahore, Indraprastha, Hastinapur, Varanasi, Prayagraj, Pataliputra, Rajgir.
Branch routes connected both highways to seaports. Uttarapatha reached the Sind and Odisha coasts. Dakshinapatha reached Virampattinam (Arikamedu) via Pratishthana.
Goods on Uttarapatha: lapis lazuli, silver and semi-precious stones from Afghanistan and Central Asia, plus sea shells from the east coast.
Rajasthan supplied semi-precious stones, silver, gold, lead, copper, iron, sandalwood and hides. Similar items appear along Dakshinapatha.
Dakshinapatha ran from Pataliputra (Magadha) to Pratishthana (Paithan). Ujjain, Vidisha and Kaushambi were key centres.

topics.title: Silk Road
notes: About 7,000 miles from China through Central Asia, north India and the Parthian Empire to Rome. Active c. 200 BC–14th century AD.
The term was coined by Carl Ritter (1838) and popularised by Ferdinand von Richthofen (1877).
Chiang Kien was sent west by Emperor Wu-ti in 138 BC with 100 men. He returned to Changan after 13 years. The Han dynasty (202 BC–220 AD) is associated with the Silk Road's rise.
It was a network of caravan routes, not one road.
Eastern terminus: Chang'an (Xian).
Western termini: Byzantium/Constantinople, Antioch, Damascus.
Gandharan art (Peshawar valley) fused Indian Buddhist art under the Kushanas with Greek art introduced by Alexander, plus some Persian elements.
The Mahabharata and Arthashastra call China "Tsin".
From China: silk, medical herbs, carved jade, furs, ceramics. To China: horses, glassware, raw jade, gold, silver.
A branch ran from Yarkand across the Karakoram to Leh and Srinagar, connecting India to the Silk Road.
Chiang Kien's report mentions India–southwest China trade via Assam and Burma in the 2nd century BC.
Literary mentions of silk:
The epics and the Manusmriti mention silk as a foreign gift.
Kautilya mentions China silk.
Kalidasa mentions Chinanashuka in Abhigyan Shakuntalam.
Xuanzang recorded Gandhara.
Kushan sites at Harwan, Ushkur and Kanispur (Kashmir) show Silk Route art influence.

topics.title: Ancient India as a trading civilization
notes: Strengths:
Strategic location
Long coastline (over 7,500 km today)
Fertile land and mineral resources
Skilled artisans
Shipbuilding
Market towns
Maritime knowledge
Trade partners: Mesopotamia, Egypt, Persia, Rome, Southeast Asia, China.
Key features: ports, road networks, merchant guilds, monsoon navigation.

topics.title: Early international trade (Akhanda Bharath)
notes: Surplus agriculture in the Indus Valley Civilization (2600–1900 BCE) led to urban centres, trade and crafts.
Harappans were seafarers, shown by boats on seals, tablets and amulets.
Panini's Uttarapatha (the Oxus–Ganges road) connected to the Achaemenid road network.
India–Babylon trade went via the Persian Gulf. Herodotus (5th century BC) attests the sea route.
The Baberu Jataka tells of Indian merchants taking a peacock by sea to Babylon.
Alexander intended to explore the south Arabian coast to link India and Egypt.

topics.title: Export portfolio
notes: Export table:
Spices: valued in Europe and West Asia
Cotton textiles: fine fabrics
Silk: luxury item
Precious stones: diamonds, sapphires, rubies
Beads: glass and semi-precious stones
Ivory: luxury decorative products
Sandalwood: fragrance and rituals
Indigo: textile dye
Sugar: India introduced sugar-making
Categories, destinations and value claims:
Spices (pepper, cardamom, cinnamon, turmeric) to Rome, Arabia, China. Valued weight-for-weight with silver.
Textiles (muslin "woven air", silk, cotton) to Rome, Persia, Southeast Asia. Egyptian mummies were wrapped in Indian cotton.
Gems (diamonds, rubies, sapphires, pearls) to Persia, Rome, China. Golconda diamonds were the global benchmark.
Manufactured goods (steel, iron tools, pottery, beads, conch shells, metalwork) to Mesopotamia, Africa, Southeast Asia. Found in Mesopotamian graves of 3000 BCE.
Luxury goods (sandalwood, indigo, perfumes, incense) to Rome, Arabia, China. Prestige material for thrones and ornaments.

topics.title: Spices
notes: Why spices were valuable: food preservation, medicine (Ayurveda), ritual, status symbol, currency substitute (the slide says pepper paid Roman soldiers; see FLAG 5).
Spice route chain:
Vasco da Gama's 1498 voyage aimed to cut out Arab middlemen.

topics.title: Textiles and gems
notes: Dhaka muslin was called "woven air". Romans called it "India fabrics". The Greek geographer Arrian described it as transparent.
Calico and chintz were named after Calicut. England passed a law in 1701 banning Indian cotton to protect local weavers.
India imported raw silk from China, added value, and re-exported finished silk to Rome and Persia.
Golconda was the only known diamond source until Brazil (1725). The Koh-i-Noor and Hope diamonds came from there.
Carnelian beads from Gujarat were found in Mesopotamian royal tombs (2600 BCE).
Gulf of Mannar pearls were a top luxury, and Rome imported pearl necklaces.

topics.title: Imports
notes: Gold and silver: India lacked major gold deposits.
Roman gold aurei are found at Tamil Nadu ports; India was a "gold sink" for Rome.
Imported gold underpinned the gold Karshapana.
A positive trade balance led to gold accumulation.
Horses: India could not breed war-quality horses.
Vijayanagara spent 15,000 gold pagodas a year on Arabian horses imported via Oman traders.
This was a strategic dependency, like modern oil.
Other imports: glass, wine and olive oil from Rome; silk from China; tin and camphor from Southeast Asia; copper from Arabia.
Roman amphorae were found at Arikamedu (Pondicherry), a Roman trading post.
Lesson: no economy is fully self-sufficient.

topics.title: Trade routes: sea, land, Periplus
notes: Indian Ocean sea route (India–Arabia–East Africa–Southeast Asia):
Used the monsoon winds "discovered" by Hippalus (1st century CE).
Ports: Calicut, Muscat, Aden, Zanzibar. Called the first "Blue Economy".
Key stops: Barygaza (Bharuch), Malabar, Ceylon, Aden/Red Sea, Alexandria.
Silk Road overland (India–Central Asia–China–Persia–Rome):
A network, not one road, with caravans of 1,000+ camels.
Key stops: Taxila, Bactria, Parthia, Antioch, Rome.
Periplus route:
The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (1st century CE) was a Greek merchant's sailing guide listing 40+ Indian ports.
Key stops: Barygaza, Kalliena, Musikanos, Patala, Barbarikon.

topics.title: Trade as an agent of cultural exchange
notes: Core idea: ideas travel with goods.
Religion: Buddhism spread along trade routes, and Borobudur is described as funded by Indian traders (see FLAG 5). Fa Xian came in 399 CE.
Language: Sanskrit spread to Southeast Asia, and Khmer, Javanese and Thai scripts derive from Indian scripts. "Shampoo" comes from champi.
Art: Gandharan art was a Greek–Indian fusion. Angkor Wat reflects Indian temple architecture.
Food: pepper went to Rome, and "curry" appears in English cookbooks by the 1600s.
Five-step mechanism: Contact → Curiosity → Adoption → Adaptation → Integration.
Buddhism case study: Theravada took local form in Sri Lanka and Thailand; Mahayana fused with Taoism in China. There are about 500 million Buddhists today.

topics.title: Trade and diplomacy ("soft power")
notes: Gift diplomacy: Chandragupta sent Seleucus I an elephant herd and received a Greek princess plus territory. This deck dates it to 321 BCE (see FLAG 2).
Merchant embassies: the Ayyavole 500 guild had its own flags and armies. Its 1067 CE inscription describes a private corporation with a foreign policy.
Royal missions: Ashoka sent missions to 5 Greek kingdoms, and Gupta kings had envoys in China and Ceylon. Xuanzang (629 CE) documented 20+ trading kingdoms, a "market research report".
Shared legal frameworks: identical standard weights in Indus cities and Mesopotamia. The Arthashastra (300 BCE) is called an "International Business Manual".

topics.title: Then vs now, and 5 lessons
notes: Analogies:
Spice monopoly → De Beers / OPEC
Ayyavole guild → MNCs
Monks → Netflix/K-pop
Periplus → Ease of Doing Business index
Gift diplomacy → Belt & Road Initiative
Ayurveda adapted for Arab markets → McAloo Tikki (glocalisation)
Lessons:

modules.title: Guild System & State Regulation of Trade

topics.title: Origin of guilds (Shrenis)
notes: Guilds arose from the need for cooperation among traders and craftsmen.
Drivers: trade expansion, occupational specialization, long-distance commerce.
Guilds united people of the same occupation for protection and benefit.
Early references: Vedic literature, the epics, Buddhist texts, Panini, the Dharmashastras.

topics.title: Membership norms
notes: Members came from the same profession, and trust had to be established first.
Admission required mutual agreement, a written constitution, acceptance by members, and guarantees or witnesses.
Members had to obey the constitution.

topics.title: Collective accountability
notes: Every member protected the guild's reputation, and decisions were binding.
Rights, duties, financial responsibilities and reputation were shared.
Guild welfare came before individual interest.

topics.title: Discipline
notes: Penalties: confiscation of property, expulsion/banishment, other punishments.
Those causing disputes or divisions were punished severely.
Guilds arbitrated members' disputes and regulated family matters affecting membership.

topics.title: Democratic character
notes: Collective decision-making, with executive officers or a committee for daily affairs.
Leaders had to be honest and capable.
The king protected guild customs and decisions.

topics.title: Public responsibility
notes: Guilds built temples, assembly halls, wells and ponds.
They provided water for travellers, supported religious ceremonies, helped the poor, and promoted education and culture.

topics.title: Price regulation
notes: Goal: fair prices for producers and consumers. Laws came from the Dharmashastras and Arthashastra.
The Panyadhyaksha (Superintendent of Commerce) set prices considering cost of production, demand and supply, transport, market conditions and reasonable profit.
Kautilya's profit caps: 5% on local goods, 10% on imported goods. Exceeding them was punished.
With excess supply, the state centralised sales and blocked parallel sales until stocks cleared.
No hoarding was allowed.
Dishonest pricing was an offence. The Jatakas mention the Agghakaraka, an official who valued goods for the king.
Prices moved from negotiated to standardized as money spread.

topics.title: Wages and retail trade
notes: There are only limited references to wages.
When goods were centralised, merchants sold for daily wages under supervision.
Retailers acted as agents of wholesalers. They handed over proceeds and agreed profits, and bore losses if market value fell.
The chapter has no separate detailed wage system.

topics.title: Weights and measures
notes: The king examined weights every six months.
The Superintendent of Weights and Measures made standard weights, then certified and stamped instruments for a fee.
Unstamped or false weights were fined. Minor accidental errors were tolerated, but deliberate fraud was punished.
Regular inspections built confidence.

topics.title: Adulteration
notes: Offences: mixing inferior with superior goods, passing off poor goods, short quantity.
Goods covered: medicines, oils, salt, perfumes, rice, molasses, earthen products, hides, threads.

topics.title: Consumer protection and the role of the state
notes: Consumer protection: profit caps, anti-hoarding and speculation controls, standard weights, adulteration penalties, retail regulation, price supervision, trader licensing.
State duties: supervise markets, fix prices, control profits, inspect weights, issue licences, prevent hoarding, ensure fair competition, protect consumers, encourage trade.

topics.title: Emergence of banking
notes: Barter gave way to surplus, markets and trade.
New needs arose: safe custody of wealth, access to credit, and financing for long-distance trade. These created the foundation for financial intermediation.

topics.title: Guilds as institutions
notes: Associations of merchants and artisans that were self-governing and recognised by the state.
Roles: trade regulation, quality control, finance, dispute resolution.
Structure: guild head, treasurer, members, apprentices.

topics.title: Guild banking and collective wealth
notes: Enabling conditions: collective wealth, growing trade, public trust, demand for organised credit.
Flow: Deposits → Guild Treasury → Loans → Trade → Repayment.
Idle funds were channelled to merchants.

topics.title: Financial intermediation
notes: Mobilising savings and lending them for productive use, connecting surplus holders with capital seekers.
Result: investment, employment, growth.
Indirect transfer: saver → intermediary → firm.

topics.title: Trust, ethics and governance
notes: Foundations: trust, Dharma, transparency, collective responsibility.
Governance: guild head, treasurer, council, member accountability.
Relevant to modern corporate governance and regulation.

topics.title: Guild banking vs modern banking
notes: Shared: deposits, loans, trade finance, records, support for development.
Modern banking differs in scale, technology, formal regulation and range of products.

topics.title: Responsible finance and financial inclusion
notes: Principles: trust, productive lending, ethical governance, inclusion.
Modern applications: ESG, responsible lending, digital banking, UPI.
Institutions must earn returns and keep public confidence.

topics.title: Dispute resolution
notes: Disputes: loan defaults, contract breaches, quality disputes, price disagreements.
Process: complaint → hearing → evidence → decision → penalty/compensation.
Modern equivalents: arbitration, banking grievance mechanisms, consumer forums.

topics.title: Instruments and historical evidence
notes: Practices: deposits, loans, interest, accounting records. Hundis were a key stage.
Sources: Arthashastra, Jataka Tales, inscriptions at Nasik, Sanchi and Mathura.

topics.title: Cooperative banking, SHGs, microfinance
notes: Parallels: collective savings, credit, peer monitoring, community development.
Outcomes: financial inclusion, women's empowerment, MSME finance.

topics.title: Credit appraisal: Ujjain merchant
notes: A merchant from Ujjain wants finance to export to Alexandria. He needs capital for raw materials, labour, transport and customs.
The lender should assess the loan's purpose, repayment ability and trade risks.

topics.title: Evolution of banking
notes: Barter → Coins → Guild Banking → Hundis → Presidency Banks → RBI → Nationalisation → Core Banking → Internet Banking → UPI → AI & Digital Banking.
Constants: deposits, lending, trust.

topics.title: Why money and ethics matter
notes: Reliable money plus ethical conduct creates trust in markets.
Trade grew from barter to international commerce.

topics.title: Barter and its problems
notes: Double coincidence of wants, indivisibility, valuation, and the need for a standard medium of exchange.

topics.title: Punch-marked coins
notes: c. 6th century BCE, made of silver with official symbols.
They eased taxation and long-distance trade and built confidence.

topics.title: Gold dinars
notes: Issued by the Kushan and Gupta dynasties.
They reflected prosperity and Roman trade, and encouraged urbanisation and specialisation.

topics.title: Standardization as the infrastructure of trust
notes: Uniform weights and measures, standard coin purity, guild certification.
Result: less fraud, lower transaction costs, more confidence.

topics.title: Ethical business principles
notes: Satya (truthfulness), Fair Pricing (avoid exploitation), Social Responsibility (wider welfare), Integrity (honour contracts).

topics.title: Dharma vs profit maximisation
notes: Dharma balances wealth with ethics and long-term stakeholder welfare.
Modern link: ESG and corporate governance.

topics.title: Modern relevance
notes: Digital payments (standardization, speed), ethical banking, consumer protection, responsible business/ESG.

topics.title: Synthesis
notes: Barter → Coins → Standards → Ethics → Trust. Matching stages: direct exchange, standardized value, comparable quality, responsible conduct, efficient markets.
Exit chain: Standardized money → lower friction → trust → ethical markets.
Four takeaways:
References: Balram Srivastava, Trade and Commerce in Ancient India; Kautilya's Arthashastra.

modules.title: State as Driver of Trade & Commerce (Mauryan Empire)

topics.title: Four roles of the state
notes: By 322 BCE Chandragupta had built the first pan-Indian empire.
The state played four roles:
Regulator: prices, weights, anti-hoarding and fraud control.
Investor: roads, ports, irrigation.
Revenue Collector: taxes on production, tolls, trade.
Diplomat: treaties and embassies.
Deck detail: Unlike earlier regional kingdoms, the Mauryan state took a direct, hands-on role in the economy rather than leaving trade to merchants and guilds alone.

topics.title: Centralized political economy
notes: Provinces were run by governors, often princes (kumaras).
The Arthashastra served as an economic governance manual.
Adhyakshas (superintendents) oversaw departments.
Gudhapurushas (spies) reported on prices, markets and officials.
Deck detail: Provincial governors (often princes) pushed decisions closer to markets; the spy network reported on prices, markets and the conduct of officials back to the centre.

topics.title: Offices and provinces
notes: Superintendents:
Panyadhyaksha: commerce
Sulkadhyaksha: tolls/customs
Pautavadhyaksha: weights and measures
Akaradhyaksha: mines (state monopoly)
Navadhyaksha: ships, ports, ferries
Capitals:
Pataliputra: imperial capital
Taxila: northwest
Ujjain: west (Malwa)
Tosali: east (Kalinga)
Suvarnagiri: south (Deccan), "mountain of gold", vital for gold and gems

topics.title: Taxation, regulation and welfare
notes: Revenue came from a share of land produce plus tolls (sulka).
Other tools: price regulation, anti-hoarding, standardized weights, measures and currency.

topics.title: Road networks
notes: Uttarapatha (Northern Route) ran from Pataliputra through Taxila to the northwest, carrying Central Asian and Hellenistic trade.
Dakshinapatha (Southern Route) linked the Gangetic plains to the Deccan, carrying gold, gems and spices.
These were a precursor to the Grand Trunk Road.
Support infrastructure: rest houses, wells, garrisoned outposts, river transport and ports, irrigation.
Deck detail: State-built roads converted scattered regional markets into one connected trading network. Irrigation along trade roads links agricultural surplus to tradeable goods.

topics.title: Diplomacy
notes: Treaty with Seleucus I Nicator (c. 303 BCE): territory up to the Hindu Kush for 500 war elephants, plus a marriage alliance (see FLAG 2).
Megasthenes was Seleucus's ambassador at Pataliputra and wrote the Indica.
Deimachus, Antiochus I's ambassador, served at Bindusara's court.
Ashoka's envoys reached five Hellenistic kings, per Rock Edict XIII: Antiochus II, Ptolemy II, Antigonus II, Magas, Alexander of Epirus.
Deck detail: Megasthenes's account, the Indica, survives only in fragments. Embassies routinely doubled as commercial and intelligence channels.

topics.title: People and dates
notes: Rulers:
Chandragupta (r. c. 322–297 BCE)
Kautilya (fl. 4th century BCE)
Bindusara (r. c. 297–268 BCE)
Ashoka (r. c. 268–232 BCE)
Timeline:
c. 303: Seleucus treaty; Megasthenes arrives
c. 261: Kalinga War → Dhamma/welfare turn
c. 250: embassies reach Hellenistic kings and Sri Lanka
c. 232: Ashoka dies
c. 185 BCE: fall of the Mauryas

topics.title: Mauryan vs modern state
notes: Centralized administration → ministries and regulators.
Roads → national highways.
Diplomacy → bilateral trade agreements.
Where the analogy breaks: adhyakshas answered to the emperor, not a legislature.
Key terms list (slide 12).

modules.title: Kushana Dynasty and the Silk Route

topics.title: "Globalization before globalization"
notes: The ancient world was economically and culturally interconnected long before container ships.

topics.title: The intermediary state
notes: After the Mauryan Empire fragmented, the Kushanas rose to prominence. They were originally the Yuezhi (Yue-chi), a nomadic clan from Central Asia.

topics.title: The geographic bridge
notes: Kujula Kadphises, Vima Kadphises and Kanishka unified Central Asia and north India.
They controlled routes from the Oxus valley (Bactria) to Mathura and Varanasi.
This made them a nexus of the Roman Empire, Han China and the Indian kingdoms.

topics.title: Kanishka and Eurasian integration
notes: Kanishka ascended c. 78 CE (see FLAG 3).
His territory ran from Tashkent and parts of Chinese Turkestan into north India.
Primary capital: Purushapura (Peshawar). Secondary centre: Mathura.
He controlled Kashgar, Yarkand, Khotan and the Pamir passes.

topics.title: Security and tolls
notes: The state secured caravan routes with supply stations and fortified posts.
It levied tolls (sulka) and cesses on luxury transit goods.

topics.title: Commodity flow
notes: Chinese silk moved through Kushan lands to Barygaza (Broach) and Barbaricum.
India added Malabar pepper ("black gold"), muslins, cotton and ivory.
Imports: Roman glass, wines, realgar, orpiment, antimony and bullion.

topics.title: Cultural diffusion
notes: Kanishka patronised Mahayana Buddhism and hosted the Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir.
Buddhism spread to China, Central Asia and Tibet.
The Gandhara School of Art blended Greco-Roman/Hellenistic style with Indian Buddhist themes.

topics.title: Evolution of Kushan coinage
notes: Kujula Kadphises: mainly copper coins, with Hellenistic designs.
Vima Kadphises: introduced gold coinage.
Kanishka: extensive gold coinage system.

topics.title: Favourable trade balance
notes: High-purity gold coins are proof of wealth and a favourable balance of trade.
Gold reserves came from tolls and from selling eastern goods for Roman bullion.

topics.title: Monetary stability
notes: Kushan dinaras matched Roman aureus weight and purity standards.
This brought Eurasian monetary stability: merchants trusted the coins, transaction risk fell, and cross-border credit became easier.

topics.title: Guild banking (Shrenis/Negamas)
notes: Guilds acted as ancient banks.
State and royal bodies deposited permanent endowments with guilds such as weavers, potters and oil-millers.
The fixed monthly interest funded public works and religious activities.

topics.title: Route mapping and the "toll gate of Eurasia"
notes: Overland route: Han China → Kashgar, Yarkand, Khotan → Bactria.
Southern branches ran along the Indus to Barbaricum (mouth of the Indus) and Barygaza (Gujarat), then to the Roman West by sea.
Wealth chain: Strategic location → control of routes → tolls → favourable balance → gold reserves → prosperity.
Final reflection, four significances: beyond infrastructure and profit; monetary and technological trust; transmitting culture and art; a channel for philosophies.

topics.title: Introduction
notes: Maritime trade is the exchange of goods and services by sea.
India's tradition is over 4,000 years old.
Coastline is given as about 7,500 km in this deck (see FLAG 1).
The Arabian Sea, Bay of Bengal and Indian Ocean linked India to Asia, Africa and Europe.
Ports were centres of commerce, culture and diplomacy. India was the hub of the Indian Ocean network.

topics.title: The state as driver of maritime trade
notes: Governments built ports, harbours, warehouses and dockyards.
Customs duties at ports were a major source of income.
Naval forces protected sea routes, and Mauryan officials supervised ports.
Satavahanas: Roman trade via western ports.
Cholas: navy securing the Bay of Bengal.
Vijayanagara: trade with Arabia, Persia and Southeast Asia.

topics.title: Ancient maritime trade
notes: Began in the Indus Valley Civilization around 2500 BCE.
Lothal (Gujarat) had one of the earliest dockyards.
Partners: Mesopotamia and the Persian Gulf.
Exports: beads, cotton textiles, pottery, precious stones. Imports: metals and luxury goods.
Shipbuilding advances enabled long-distance voyages.

topics.title: Merchant guilds
notes: Ayyavole 500 (Ainnurruvar), Manigramam and Anjuvannam.
They set up centres in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, financed voyages and managed risk.
They maintained standards, negotiated privileges and tax concessions with rulers, and built temples, rest houses and warehouses.
Described as medieval-period institutions.

topics.title: Trade with Southeast Asia
notes: Partners: Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Cambodia, Vietnam. Kingdoms: Srivijaya, Majapahit, Khmer.
Exports: cotton textiles, spices, sandalwood, ivory, gems, metalware, handicrafts.
Imports: camphor, aromatic woods, cloves, nutmeg, tin, forest products.
Guild settlements were established.
Cultural spread: Hinduism, Buddhism, Sanskrit, Indian art. Temples: Angkor Wat, Prambanan.
Indian administration, law and education were adopted.

topics.title: Trade with China
notes: Via the Maritime Silk Route; expanded under the Tang and Song dynasties.
India exported spices, cotton, indigo, medicinal herbs, ivory, gems and aromatics.
China exported silk, porcelain, paper and tea.
Faxian (Fa-Hien) and Xuanzang (Hiuen Tsang) documented Indian commercial centres.
Monks and scholars carried Buddhist exchange.

topics.title: Trade with Arabia and West Asia
notes: Via the Arabian Sea, with Oman, Yemen, Bahrain and Persia.
Arab traders linked India to Mediterranean and European markets.
Exports: pepper, cardamom, cotton, indigo, sandalwood, ivory, gems, sugar.
Imports: Arabian horses, dates, pearls, gold, silver, perfumes.
Muslim merchant communities settled in Gujarat, Kerala and the Konkan.

topics.title: Major commodities
notes: Pepper was the "Black Gold".
Other exports: cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, textiles, silk, indigo, sandalwood, ivory, pearls, gems, steel, handicrafts, herbs.
Imports: gold, silver, copper, tin, coral, horses, wine, glassware, Chinese silk and porcelain.

topics.title: Economic and cultural impact
notes: Port cities: Muziris, Bharuch, Kaveripattinam.
Jobs for merchants, sailors, shipbuilders, artisans and labourers.
Customs revenue funded administration, and commercial wealth funded temples and education.
Spread of Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism.
Foreign communities increased diversity in port cities.

topics.title: Arrival of Europeans
notes: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498, a turning point.
The Portuguese set up at Goa, Cochin and Diu, followed by the Dutch, English and French.
Europeans brought monopolies and naval conflicts.
Trade shifted to European control, laying the foundation for colonial domination.

topics.title: Maritime heritage
notes: Knowledge of navigation, astronomy, currents and monsoons.
Stitched-plank shipbuilding.
Evidence: ports, inscriptions, coins, temples, archaeology.
Government revival initiatives.

topics.title: INSV Kaundinya
notes: A modern reconstruction of an ancient stitched-plank vessel, built with coir stitching and wooden planks and no metal fasteners.
It retraced the India–Oman route.
Purposes: research, cultural diplomacy, heritage revival.
